3edfea80-630c-4a6c-b385-6c146842b3fa.one_liner: A scenario-planning piece on diesel spiking to $8-10/gal ties energy-driven CPI pressure to a resurging Fed hawkish bias (2yr yield vs WTI correlation) and warns the ultimate macro effect is demand destruction/recession risk, not persistent inflation.
3edfea80-630c-4a6c-b385-6c146842b3fa.recap: The piece argues policymakers and markets should start treating $8-10/gallon diesel as a real scenario rather than clickbait. National average diesel hit roughly $6.20/gallon (AAA), with California near $8 and isolated stations at $9.99. The bottleneck isn't crude supply but refining and distribution: Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries, a Russian diesel export ban, and Middle East refining/shipping disruption (including Strait of Hormuz risk) have squeezed finished-fuel output even as crack spreads surge to extraordinary levels, though refineries can't quickly expand capacity. Options like export bans, tax suspensions, or reserve releases only reshuffle costs rather than adding supply, and an export ban specifically risks raising gasoline prices 15-30 cents/gallon by industry estimates. If refiners tilt output toward diesel/heating oil for winter, gasoline supply tightens too, potentially compounding pressure on consumers as summer 2026 EIA gasoline-supplied data already showed weaker demand than 2024/2025. The host highlights that the 2-year Treasury yield has re-correlated with WTI since Jackson Hole, jumping from 4.2% to above 4.7% in about three weeks, reflecting market pricing of a more hawkish Fed reacting to energy-driven headline CPI, even though rate hikes can't fix refining capacity. Drawing a parallel to the 1990-91 recession triggered by the Iraq-Kuwait oil shock, the argument concludes energy shocks don't cause lasting inflation spirals — they raise prices short-term but ultimately destroy demand, compress margins, and cost jobs across trucking, construction, farming, and retail.
terms: WTI -- West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark crude oil price
Crack spread -- the difference between the cost of crude oil and the wholesale price of refined products like diesel, used as a proxy for refining margins

80a4d226-341e-4036-9e5f-7a0c6ea536e7.recap: Chris Whalen reacts to a 25bp Fed hike, calling it 'pretty lame' and largely symbolic, arguing the Fed is now the 'tail' to Treasury's 'dog' given a $2 trillion annual deficit (~6% of GDP) that dwarfs monetary policy's influence. He expects inflation to stay persistent, driven by energy (oil above $100, diesel shortages tied to Middle East conflict and Houthi disruption of the Red Sea), and predicts the Fed will eventually be forced back into QE/debt monetization since Congress won't cut the deficit. He notes corporate bond spreads have compressed even as rates rise, meaning investors are still buying paper despite funding stress in non-bank sectors. A large chunk of the conversation covers private credit's spillover into life insurers: firms like Guggenheim and 777 allegedly loaded insurance balance sheets with leveraged, dubious private-credit assets to boost equity returns beyond normal 12-15%, and Whalen expects failures, litigation, and state guaranty funds having to absorb failed carriers, with annuity holders potentially losing money. He also flags housing: over half of US homes fell in price over the trailing year, predicting a broader correction through 2028. On rates trading, he discusses bank deposit costs turning up after six quarters of decline (Wells Fargo, Fifth Third, Huntington) and details why he holds Annaly (MBS/Treasury spread, low prepayment speeds, MSR book) and AGNC, plus commentary on SEC crypto rulemaking and gold as a portfolio hedge.

cb320557-3e95-4758-a395-588405337a43.one_liner: Fitch's record 6.3% private-credit default rate is largely a maturity-extension/liquidity story, not a wave of outright defaults, but it's spilling into real-estate fund redemptions, insurance-company affiliated-loan scrutiny (Mark Walter/TWG), and a $22bn bank bridge loan for an AI chip deal awaiting bond-market takeout.
cb320557-3e95-4758-a395-588405337a43.recap: The piece argues private credit's record 6.3% trailing-12-month default rate (Fitch, 1,300 US borrowers, August) understates the real story: 45% of August defaults were stressed maturity extensions, not missed payments, meaning lenders roll loans because borrowers can't refinance or sell. That traps lender cash — sometimes converted to payment-in-kind interest (Houlihan Lokey: 11.8% of loans by size took some PIK in Q2, 6.3% of interest dollars) — so reported income diverges from cash income. Floating-rate exposure plus sticky Fed policy squeezes highly leveraged borrowers' thin interest coverage. The stress is worst among smaller borrowers: loans to $10-20mm EBITDA companies trading below 90 cents on the dollar rose from ~1% in 2023 to 12% now; $20-100mm EBITDA borrowers hit 6% (three-year high); >$100mm borrowers only 3%. Healthcare and industrial manufacturing led sector defaults at 9.9%; software defaults fell to 0.6% but valuations face AI-disruption risk. The same liquidity crunch shows up elsewhere: Blackstone and Invesco face redemption pressure and are arranging secondary sales/fee cuts in open-ended real estate funds (Blackstone's BPP fund, ~$11bn NAV); Mark Walter's TWG-controlled insurers (Delaware Life, Clear Spring) disclosed over $20bn of previously misclassified affiliated loans amid regulatory scrutiny, prompting Walter to sell the LA Lakers and explore selling Chelsea stakes; and ten banks are bridging a $22bn loan for Blackstone/Alphabet's Crux AI Google-TPU venture, intended to later be refinanced in the IG bond market. SoftBank's 5-year CDS hit its highest level since 2023 on OpenAI-related exposure concerns. The author frames all this as capital being rationed rather than disappearing.

ecca2862-b38a-11f1-8ba3-5bdd634cc779.implications: For a repo/financing desk, the key read-throughs are: (1) natural real-money demand for 20-30yr paper is structurally shrinking as insurers rotate into floating-rate private credit, which argues for a steeper curve and higher term premium absent a risk-off catalyst; (2) Treasury's buyback/TGA mechanics are a liquidity-support and optics tool for off-the-runs, not a genuine debt-reduction or funding-supply relief valve, so don't expect it to ease bill/bond supply dynamics materially; (3) continued heavy IG corporate issuance for AI capex is a direct competitor for balance sheet against Treasuries, relevant to swap spreads and asset-swap levels.

ecca2862-b38a-11f1-8ba3-5bdd634cc779.one_liner: A fixed-income CIO walks through why the long end is selling off, how insurance companies have quietly swapped natural long-Treasury demand for floating-rate private credit, and the mechanics (and limits) of Treasury's new buyback program.
ecca2862-b38a-11f1-8ba3-5bdd634cc779.recap: David Bush, CIO of Trajan Wealth and a former 18-year bond portfolio manager, discusses the six-month bond selloff (10-year up ~60bp, 30-year near 5.29% after crossing 5.3% in August). He attributes rising yields to $40 trillion in outstanding Treasury debt, tariff- and Iran-conflict-driven inflation, and heavy IG corporate issuance funding AI capex, which crowds out Treasury demand. The most detailed section covers the shifting buyer base for long-duration government paper: insurance companies, pensions and sovereign wealth funds are the natural buyers of 20-30 year bonds, but insurers have been reallocating a portion (roughly 7-15% of assets, per his due diligence) into private credit, which is largely floating-rate and thus near-zero duration, while keeping the rest of the book duration-matched to liabilities. He frames this as insurers dialing down duration and convexity risk while dialing up credit and liquidity risk to chase yield, and flags due-diligence concerns (loan tape access, delinquency data, interval-fund redemption gates capped near 5% of NAV per quarter). He then explains Treasury's buyback program in detail: increased from $2B to $4B (with $6B actually executed September 9), potentially funded via the TGA, aimed at supporting liquidity in illiquid off-the-run issues; he notes it can reduce headline notional debt (buying bonds back at a discount to par and reissuing at par) without materially changing total interest cost. The episode closes with views on gold/dollar dynamics, AI-driven equity sectors, and private credit skepticism generally.
terms: TGA -- Treasury General Account, the U.S. Treasury's operating cash account held at the Federal Reserve
on-the-run/off-the-run -- the most recently issued Treasury benchmark (on-the-run) versus previously issued, less liquid issues of the same maturity (off-the-run)
BDC -- Business Development Company, a publicly listed or private vehicle that lends to and invests in mid-sized companies
REO -- Real Estate Owned, property a lender has foreclosed on and taken onto its books
loan tape -- a schedule/data file listing the individual loans in a credit portfolio, including performance and delinquency status
